LET US PUT THE FACTS ON THE TABLE: THE KARIBA TRAGEDY AND THE GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE
dignity and answers.

While we mourn,we must also be honest about the https://t.co/jTEkpWXH3K is unfair to claim that the Government did absolutely nothing in response to this tragedy.

1. The President declared a National State of Disaster.

On 12 August 2026, President Emmerson Mnangagwa declared the Kariba ferry tragedy a State of Disaster under Section 27(1) of the Civil Protection Act [Chapter 10:06].

This was not merely a statement of sympathy.The declaration enabled Government to mobilise extraordinary resources for rescue operations,recovery and humanitarian assistance to affected families.

2. A national search-and-rescue operation was activated.

The Department of Civil Protection coordinated operations involving:

- The @PoliceZimbabwe Sub-Aqua Unit.
- The @ArmyZimbabwe Boat Squadron.
- Local authorities and other stakeholders.
- A privately owned helicopter from the Matusadona Conservation Trust.

Seventy-seven people were rescued. Search and recovery teams worked under extremely difficult conditions to retrieve victims and account for those missing.

3. The @ZimFirstLady personally visited the bereaved families.

On 19 August 2026,Dr Auxillia Mnangagwa travelled to Kariba to meet grieving families and survivors. She listened to their experiences, offered condolences,comforted the bereaved and stood with the community during a deeply painful period.

She also recognised Taurai Chalibamba ,whose extraordinary bravery saved seven lives,with a cash gift.

Importantly,the @ZimFirstLady conveyed the President @edmnangagwa 's condolences and made it clear that Government stood with the affected community.

It is therefore factually incorrect to suggest that no senior national representative visited the grieving families.

4. Government provided tangible humanitarian assistance.

The response did not end with the rescue operation.

By September 2026, Government had reported the following interventions:

- More than 75 tonnes of mealie-meal and rice provided to affected families and communities.
- 60 tonnes of mealie-meal specifically earmarked for ferry disaster victims, from a wider allocation of 200 tonnes for Kariba District.
- Cash transfers and livelihood support measures announced.
- Psychosocial support and counselling for survivors and affected families.
- Educational assistance through the Basic Education Assistance Module (BEAM) for eligible children.
- Medical assistance for those requiring treatment.
- State-assisted funeral arrangements through Doves and Nyaradzo Funeral Services.

Cabinet also approved a broader humanitarian recovery programme covering mental health, children's welfare, emergency supplies and livelihood restoration.

These are documented interventions, not political slogans.

5. Government has taken steps to restore the community's transport services.

On 12 September, Government announced the certification of a replacement ferry offered by a private operator and confirmed that two additional vessels were being procured.

The recovery programme also included road rehabilitation, improved weather monitoring, water safety training and stronger emergency preparedness.

6. What about the Mafusire Commission?

Let us be accurate here too.

On 13 October 2026, the Board of Inquiry chaired by Supreme Court Justice Joseph Mafusire formally commenced its work.

Its mandate includes investigating:

- The vessel's registration,certification and seaworthiness.
- Its passenger and cargo capacity.
- The competence of those responsible for its procurement and operation.
- The conduct of the authorities responsible for inland water transport.
- Whether proper safety procedures and weather warnings were observed.

The commission has the authority to summon witnesses,hear testimony and make recommendations.

The fact that the inquiry has been established does not mean that accountability has already been achieved.

text:
The House does not acquit Hegseth, it postpones the reckoning

The House of Representatives did not decide whether Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had committed high crimes and misdemeanours, as the House did not vote on the substance of the charges. The House voted instead on whether it would be required to decide the question at all, and it decided that it would not be required to decide it in this Congress.

By a vote of 211 to 204, the House adopted a motion to refer H. Res. 1655, which is the impeachment resolution against Hegseth, to the House Judiciary Committee. The motion to reconsider was then laid on the table, which means that the referral stands as the final action of the House on the matter for the present session.

The recorded breakdown of the vote was as follows - Republicans voted 210 in favour of referral and 1 against referral, Democrats voted 0 in favour of referral and 203 against referral and the Independent member voted in favour of referral - the total result was 211 yeas, 204 nays, 18 not voting with 2 vacancies.

[The sole Republican who voted against referral was Rep.Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who introduced the resolution.]

✲ Procedure became the verdict: Massie filed the resolution on Monday, 9 Nov, as a privileged resolution u/the rules of the House. A privileged resolution requires House l/ship to act within 2-legislative days, and l/ship may choose among three options, which are to permit a direct vote on the articles, to table the resolution, or to refer the resolution to committee.

Republican l/ship chose the third option, which was referral, and the motion to refer was offered by Rep.Darrell Issa.

[Referral was the least visible of the three options, and it was also the most effective option for preventing a direct vote, as a direct vote on the articles would have required only a simple majority to impeach, whereas referral required only a simple majority to avoid a direct vote.]

The practical consequence of referral is that the articles now rest with the Judiciary Committee, which is controlled by allies of Pres.D.Trump. The committee is not expected to take up the articles before the current Congress ends on 3 Jan. When the current Congress ends, the articles will formally expire, and Democrats, who will take control of the House in Jan, would be required to introduce a new resolution if they wish to revive the impeachment effort in the new Congress.

[The vote was therefore not an acquittal, and it was not a finding of innocence, as it was a deferral that extends beyond the point at which this House can act.]

✲ What Massie alleges - 8-Articles in full: The resolution contains eight articles of impeachment, and it is essential to state with precision that these articles are allegations made by Massie, and they are not findings by a committee, and they are not rulings by a court. Hegseth rejects all of the allegations, and he has described the entire effort as a farce.

The first three articles concern the war against Iran, which began on 28 Feb with joint American and Is*aeli strikes. Article I alleges that Hegseth waged war without a declaration of war, without congressional authorisation, without an attack on the United States, and without an imminent threat to the United States. Article II alleges that Hegseth continued the war after both chambers of Congress passed a measure directing the withdrawal of American forces under the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Article III alleges that Hegseth continued the war beyond the 60-day limit established by the War Powers Resolution, and beyond the additional thirty-day withdrawal period permitted by that law.

Article IV alleges that Hegseth dismantled legal safeguards intended to limit civilian casualties, and it cites a strike on a school in Minab, Iran, which the resolution states k.illed at least 156 people, most of whom were children - k.illed or injured over 200 in total.

Article V alleges extrajudicial killings in the campaign against suspected drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean Sea and the Eastern Pacific Ocean, and it states that the strikes k.illed at least 243 people, and that the campaign included strikes on survivors and failures to rescue survivors.

Article VI alleges that Hegseth used Pentagon authority to retaliate against Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona for speaking publicly about unlawful military orders.

Article VII alleges the unlawful seizure of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores, and it describes that operation as the kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader without legal authority.

Article VIII alleges that Hegseth authorised military operations in Yemen without congressional authorisation, and that he failed to provide the war powers reports that the law requires.

Massie first filed the same 34-page resolution on 15 Sep and read it aloud on the House floor. Speaker Mike Johnson then sent the House home before the procedural clock expired, which prevented a vote at that time. Massie refiled the resolution when Congress returned after the midterm elections, on the first day of the lame-duck session.

✲ Defence offered by Hegseth and Trump: Hours before the vote, Hegseth held his first Pentagon press conference in more than 180-days. At that press conference, he called the impeachment effort a farce, and he described Massie as one disgruntled and defeated congressman, and he defended the Iran war and the boat strikes as a lawful operation.

Trump defended Hegseth in the strongest terms, and he stated that Hegseth had won 2-wars, and he criticised Massie personally. Speaker Mike Johnson opposed impeachment in the middle of hostilities abroad, and he stated that impeachment would be a terrible thing for allies and enemies to see.

The argument advanced by the administration is not that Congress has no role in decisions concerning war, but that impeachment is the wrong instrument, at the wrong moment, against the wrong official, for military operations that the executive regards as lawful and necessary. The argument advanced by Massie is the older constitutional argument, which holds that the power to take the country to war belongs to Congress, and that the erosion of that power cannot be remedied by deference to the executive branch’s assurance that its actions were lawful.

✲ What the vote does not resolve: The historical rarity of the proceeding signifies its gravity, as only two Cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached by the House in American history. The first was Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876, who was impeached unanimously after resigning over a kickback scheme involving trading posts at Fort Sill, and who was later acquitted by the Senate, with a majority voting to convict but not the two-thirds required. The second was Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024, who was impeached by a vote of 214 to 213 over border enforcement, and whose articles were then dismissed by the Senate without a full trial. If Hegseth had been impeached, he would have become the third Cabinet secretary to be impeached, and the second Secretary of War to hold that distinction after Belknap.

✲ Deeper question remains unanswered: The vote therefore leaves the substantive questions entirely untouched, as it does not determine whether the War Powers Resolution still constrains a president who chooses to act without Congress, and it does not determine what constitutes lawful targeting at sea, and it does not determine what duty is owed to survivors of a strike, and it does not determine the limits of civilian protection in a war conducted largely from the air.

What the vote does determine is that this House, in its final weeks, would not force those questions to a vote.

The context for the vote is the midterm election one week earlier, in which about six in ten voters told the AP Voter Poll that the United States made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran. Massie sought to convert that public discontent into a constitutional reckoning, and his own party, with a single exception, used procedure to prevent that reckoning from taking place.

The House did not vindicate Hegseth, and the House did not condemn Hegseth, as the House declined to judge him. The House protected him from a vote that its leadership was not prepared to lose, and the House left the reckoning to a future Congress, to a future Senate, and to a public whose judgment, for now, remains o/side the chamber.

I asked Grok about this teacher and class: may be inaccurate so 🤷🏻‍♀️. We can still have opinions about regardless. 

“Analysis: Dr. Laura Yakas, SW505 — “Engaging Social Justice, Diversity, and Oppression in Social Work,” University of Michigan School of Social Work
What she teaches. SW505 is a required three-credit foundation course for the MSW program. The official description frames it around CSWE accreditation competencies: engaging diversity and difference, advancing human rights and social and economic justice, understanding power and oppression across micro, mezzo, and macro levels. Topics include types and sources of power, social locations, social constructions, identity, and self-reflexivity. Yakas’s own materials and public statements add a disability-justice and “healing-centered” lens, and she describes her pedagogy as “transformative.” She is also a performing musical comedian whose Fringe shows cover the same themes — her own words: “if you take my social justice class, subtract the articles and slides, and add swearing and singing, you get one of my shows.”
What students think. Rate My Professors shows 4.3 out of 5 with 75% saying they’d take her again. Praise centers on readings, flexibility, and engagement; criticism centers on a one-credit course that couldn’t be taken pass/fail. She received the School of Social Work’s 2024 Distinguished Lecturer Award, a peer-voted honor. The viral clip is one moment from one online section — real, but not the whole course.
Is it relevant to becoming a social worker? The underlying content has deep roots. Social work schools taught race and social-change courses in the 1970s–90s; CSWE added oppression and social-justice content to accreditation standards in 1994; the NASW Code of Ethics has required promoting social justice since 1997. A 1986 survey found 37% of grad programs had a social-justice concentration and half offered at least one such course. What is newer is the explicit language — “anti-racism,” “intersectionality,” “anti-oppressive practice” — which entered CSWE standards mainly in the 2022 revision after 2020. One 2022 analysis found that forthright terms like “racism” and “oppression” were uncommon in social work course language before 2020 and became pervasive after.
The fair questions. Whether a required, no-opt-out course taught through a single ideological frame serves students or clients is a values judgment, not a factual one. Social work has always been a values-driven profession with an explicit justice mission — that is not new. The debate is over method, balance, and whether the current packaging produces better practitioners or just more polarized ones. Nineteen states have passed laws restricting DEI content in higher ed, and CSWE is revising its 2029 standards partly in response, which suggests the tension is being worked out in real time rather than settled.”

text:
Joel Osteen’s megachurch reported $600,000 stolen from its safe. Seven years later, a plumber found hundreds of envelopes hidden behind a bathroom toilet.

In March 2014, Lakewood Church in Houston reported that $600,000 had vanished from its safe: $200,000 in cash and $400,000 in checks from weekend services. The envelopes holding financial information were gone too.

Police got nowhere. The church offered a combined $25,000 reward.

Then, on November 10, 2021, plumber Justin Cauley came to fix a loose toilet. He pulled it out and opened the wall around it.

Hundreds of envelopes fell out of the insulation. Around 500.

Inside were cash, checks and money orders. Cauley reported it to his supervisor, then called a local radio station to explain what he’d found.

Some check dates suggested a link to the 2014 theft. Police reopened the case and said the discovery appeared connected.

But nobody publicly confirmed how much was recovered. The full $600,000 was never shown to be in that wall.

And whoever hid it was never identified.

Cauley told a local TV station he expected a reward for turning it in. In December 2021, Crime Stoppers of Houston gave him $20,000.

Seven years of silence, ended by a routine plumbing job.

The plumber got $20,000. The thief got away.

Who hid $600,000 inside the walls of one of America’s biggest churches, and why did they never come back for it?

text:
With these principles in mind, in determining the threshold issue of justiciability, we scrutinize each claim individually. Indeed, in our system of separation of powers, we should not abdicate the court's Article III responsibility-the resolution of “cases” and “controversies”-in favor of the Executive Branch, particularly where, as here, the Executive has declined a long-standing invitation to involve itself in the dispute. We conclude that some of the claims are barred by the political question doctrine and some of the claims are justiciable. Although the parties have multiple procedural and substantive challenges to overcome down the road, they are entitled to their day-or years-in court on the justiciable claims.

A group of twenty-four individuals and four organizations (the “Holocaust Survivors”) claim that the Vatican Bank, known by its official title Istituto per le Opere di Religione, the Order of Friars Minor, and the Croatian Liberation Movement (Hrvatski Oslobodilacki Pokret ), profited from the genocidal acts of the Croatian Ustasha political regime (the “Ustasha”), which was supported throughout World War II by Nazi forces. That profit allegedly passed through the Vatican Bank in the form of proceeds from looted assets and slave labor. The Holocaust Survivors brought suit in federal court claiming conversion, unjust enrichment, restitution, the right to an accounting, and human rights violations and violations of international law arising out of the defendants' alleged involvement with the Ustasha during and following World War II.

 The Vatican Bank and the Order of Friars Minor moved to dismiss the Holocaust Survivors' complaint on multiple grounds; by agreement of the parties the district court limited its discussion to the issue of whether the Holocaust Survivors' claims should be dismissed under the political question doctrine. The district court reasoned that the political question doctrine bars consideration of the merits of the claims in their entirety. The district court dismissed the action against the Croatian Liberation Movement, which never appeared in the action, on the grounds that the claims were barred by both the political question doctrine and the lack of personal jurisdiction over this defendant. We reverse in part because certain of the Holocaust Survivors' claims-those with respect to lost and looted property (conversion, unjust enrichment, restitution, and an accounting)-are not barred by this doctrine. In contrast, the broad human rights allegations tied to the Vatican Bank's alleged assistance to the war objectives of the Ustasha present nonjusticiable controversies. Like the district court, we hold that the court did not have personal jurisdiction over the Croatian Liberation Movement.1 Consequently, we see no reason to reach the political question doctrine vis-à-vis this defendant.

 Bearing in mind that “[t]he decision to deny access to judicial relief is not one we make lightly,” Liu v. Republic of China, 892 F.2d 1419, 1433 (9th Cir.1989) (quoting Int'l Ass'n of Machinists & Aerospace Workers v. OPEC, 649 F.2d 1354, 1360 (9th Cir.1981)), we conclude that the political question doctrine does not create an absolute barrier to the Holocaust Survivors' property claims. To conclude otherwise would be to shirk our judicial role as “[c]ourts in the United States have the power, and ordinarily the obligation, to decide cases and controversies properly presented to them.” W.S. Kirkpatrick & Co. v. Envtl. Tectonics Corp., Int'l, 493 U.S. 400, 409, 110 S.Ct. 701, 107 L.Ed.2d 816 (1990).

That said, it bears noting that our initial determination of justiciability in no way reflects any judgment on the threshold legal hurdles that must be overcome or the merits of the claims. Much of the dissent focuses on downstream issues related to potential procedural and substantive pitfalls of the claims. We do not discount the difficulties that may lie ahead; however, consideration of those issues is premature. Given the passage of time, the generality of the allegations, the question of the applicability of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, intricacies of the alleged claims, the class certification issues, whether the claimants have a cognizable legal claim, and a myriad of other procedural and jurisdictional hurdles, the Holocaust Survivors may indeed face an uphill battle in pursuing their claims. But this spectre of difficulty down the road does not inform our justiciability determination at this early stage of the proceedings.

Our conclusion is rooted in the principles of Baker v. Carr. Despite the dissent's cataclysmic and speculative projections about the sweep of our opinion, our decision boils down to letting the common law property claims proceed to the next stage and foreclosing the political, human rights, and war-related claims. In so doing, we respect the limits of our jurisdiction as a national court, recognize the role of the Executive in foreign relations, and stick to our role of interpreting the law.

SWISS GUARD CALLED TRAITOR FOR EXPOSING BANK SCANDAL
By
PUBLISHED: May 30, 1999 at 4:00 AM EDT | UPDATED: September 24, 2021 at 12:59 AM EDT
In 1997, while working as a security guard at a Swiss bank, Christophe Meile stumbled across Holocaust-era financial documents in the bank’s shredding room. Recognizing they were documents detailing deposits made by Jews during WWII, Meile, 31, took the books home and then turned them in to a local Jewish organization in Zurich.

Meile thought his good deed would end there. But soon he was caught in the whirlwind when local authorities accused him of violating Swiss banking laws — and he was fired.

The books became proof that Switzerland’s banks and government were anything but neutral during WWII.

In his country, Meile became an outcast. He and his family fled after death threats were made against them.

His testimony in the United States spurred a class action lawsuit by Holocaust survivors that resulted in a $1.25 billion settlement last year with three Swiss banks. Meile now lives in New Jersey with his wife Guiseppina, 6-year-old daughter Miriam and 4-year-old son David. He plans to move to California where he will go to school, although he’s not sure what he will study. He also travels around the country, speaking about his experiences. Earlier this week, he visited South Florida.

Q: When you first saw those documents that detailed Jewish holdings in the banks, did you think about what telling would mean?

A: I knew it would have an impact. But on the other hand, it made more sense to preserve every evidence. I turned it over to help the Jewish people. At the time, the World Jewish Congress was pressuring Switzerland to disclose how much money they had from Jews in Swiss bank accounts. So when the finding of the documents became public, the Swiss people went crazy.

Q: What was the initial response?

A: People were angry that I helped the Jews. They told me: “You’re stupid. You don’t know what they’re like. Jewish people are bad.” I was shocked. I’m not even Jewish. I’m Swiss. I feel I did something good. For the Swiss people, I violated Swiss bank laws; I stole the documents; I’m a criminal and a traitor. Most Swiss people feel like that. They don’t agree it was a good thing like the public here in the United States does.

Q: Why do you think they reacted that way?

A: What I did was good for the United States and other countries but not for Switzerland. The Swiss don’t know about genocide. You would think they have the education about the Holocaust. I learned the most about it when I came here to the United States, when I talked to Holocaust victims. After World War II, the whole world changed, but in Switzerland, nothing happened. The whole system moved forward. There was no rebuilding of the country. The old Swiss leaders are still in power. Society was never pushed to think about what their leaders did during the Holocaust. The neutrality was for the normal people. It sounds so good, but for the business society it meant making deals with both sides. It was a tool for business.

Q: When you felt you did the right thing, others called you a traitor. Do you feel like a traitor?

A: You feel they just don’t get it. Germany, France, everybody else understood. People called me to congratulate me, to invite me to speak at events. Only the Swiss went crazy. Today, I still don’t understand. They don’t believe that the Swiss banks, the government were deeply convicted and thinking like the Nazis. People don’t want to believe that the business society worked hand in hand with the Nazis. They can’t believe they’ve been manipulated.

Q: Why did you speak up and not walk away from those documents about to be destroyed?

A: First of all, I’m a Christian. I believe the Bible is true and that Jesus is the Messiah, the boss. If you take him in your heart, he’ll give you a new life. But I also grew up different than the other kids around me. My parents divorced when I was 10. I felt discriminated by being in a family without a father. Maybe this turned me into who I am.

Q: What has your life been like in the U.S.?

A: I like it more here than in Switzerland. People here are more relaxed. They understand what I did. People here respect when someone does something good. I like the openness of American society. People let you breathe here. In Switzerland people attack you. They don’t like people who are different.

For the past two years, I worked on settling the class-action lawsuit case to bring Swiss banks to the negotiation table. I made a decent living from making speeches. I worked as a security guard in New York City for one year, standing at the door. It bored me. Now we’re moving to California. I’m trying to move on, going to a four-year college on a scholarship. I’m happy about that. I live in a two-bedroom apartment in New Jersey, but I think we’ll have more space in California. My wife works as a clerk at my attorney’s office. Now I have a pretty normal life.

Q: You’ve been called a hero by those who praise what you did. Do you feel like one?

A: No. I feel like a normal person. I think that everybody can do something like I did. Everyone has this kind of opportunity.

Q: Have you ever returned to Switzerland?

A: I returned one time to Switzerland for an interview. I stayed at a hotel and had two bodyguards. It was crazy. I wanted to explain to the Swiss people why I did what I did.

Q: Did you succeed in explaining your motives?

A: I don’t think so. A few weeks ago, I posted something on a Swiss related chat room on the Internet and the response back was incredible. One person wrote: “Christophe Meile don’t think you’re still O.K.” I got very angry comments.

Q: What are your feelings for Switzerland now?

A: I’m disappointed. I have trouble with the government there, how they manipulate the people and how the banks control Switzerland. The people are good, but they’ve been used. I can’t go back there. It’s not possible. The banks say I’m the bad guy. People feel that their tax money is paying for the settlement. I don’t feel welcome there. The problem is so long as the government doesn’t apologize in public, the Swiss people will believe that the government and the banks are right and that the Jewish people want to take over the financial power in Switzerland and that Meile helped in that.

How the Vatican's finances work
March 19, 2013, 5:30 AM PDT
By Deborah Caldwell
As Pope Francis assumes leadership of the world's 1.2 billion Catholics, he's got his work cut out for him on many fronts, not the least of which is the Vatican's finances.

Last year, a sheaf of documents was leaked by Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI's former butler in a scandal known as the Vatileaks affair. The documents allegedly showed, for example, tens of millions of dollars in transfers to American dioceses to help pay legal settlements -- estimated to have cost the American church more than $3 billion so far -- surrounding the priest sex-abuse scandals.

During his eight-year tenure, Benedict reportedly made progress toward reforming the Vatican Bank, replacing its president and creating a financial-intelligence committee. But by most accounts, the Vatican Bank still needs greater scrutiny and transparency.

So what is the Vatican Bank, and how is it related to the Catholic Church, and to the finances of Vatican City, a sovereign state? CNBC explains.

What is the Vatican Bank?
It's definitely not your average bank. Officially called the Institute for the Works of Religion, the Vatican Bank is a privately held firm run by a CEO who reports to a committee of cardinals and the Pope. It offers ATMs with transactions in Latin and boasts a small castle-like headquarters protected by Swiss Guards.

It has about 33,000 accounts, a distribution network in more than 100 countries, and an estimated $8 billion in assets. (By contrast, JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank, has about $2 trillion in assets.)

Details of the account holders are private, though the Vatican says most of the accounts belong to members of the clergy. Because its assets are not the property of the Holy See, it isn't overseen by the Vatican; instead it's considered a charitable foundation affiliated with the Vatican.

What's the controversy about the Vatican Bank?
Where do we begin? It's been controversial for decades, accused of money-laundering and collaborating with the mafia, and before that with the Nazis.

In 1982, the Vatican Bank dealt with its most serious crisis. Roberto Calvi, known as "God's Banker," was found dead, hanging from Blackfriars Bridge in London. At first his death appeared to be a suicide, but eventually five people -- including a mafia member -- were charged with his murder. Calvi was chairman of Banco Ambrosiano, which collapsed after $1.3 billion in loans disappeared; the loans had been made to dummy companies owned by the Vatican Bank, and the Vatican had provided the letters of credit.

More recently, in 2010, the Italian government launched an investigation into the bank's operations after the Bank of Italy alerted police to two suspicious Vatican Bank transactions totaling $30 million. The money was being sent from Credito Artigianato to JP Morgan Chase and another Italian bank, Banca del Fucino. The Vatican Bank apparently didn't disclose the origin of the money, which is a violation of Italian law. Ultimately, the bank denied wrongdoing and the funds were eventually released.

In December 2010, Benedict XVI established the Financial Information Authority as an independent agency to monitor the financial activities of the Vatican Bank and other Vatican-related institutions. Benedict also worked to get the Vatican on to the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development's "white list" of countries that follow international banking standards.

But the 2012 release of leaked documents — the Vatileaks affair — showed the bank was still struggling with corruption, apparently transferring tens of millions of dollars to American dioceses to help them pay child sex-abuse legal bills. There was also a letter from a senior Vatican official, Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano, in which he apparently complained of money-laundering and corruption in the Vatican.

Last May, the bank's president, Ettore Gotti Tedeschi, was ousted by the board of directors, accused of money-laundering and not following laws that block financing terrorists and criminal gangs. Tedeschi countered, saying he was fired for getting "too close to the truth."

In January, Italy stopped allowing its banks to do business with the Holy See because of the Vatican Bank's lack of financial transparency. As a result, the Italian banks cut off credit-card processing at tourist spots such as the Sistine Chapel. Some weeks later, plastic was restored after a Swiss firm that doesn't have to abide by EU banking laws came to the rescue.

Then, just before he abdicated the papacy in February, Benedict appointed a new Vatican Bank president, Ernst von Freyberg, a German-born lawyer.

How does this mess impact Pope Francis?
The cardinals will expect Francis to clean up the scandal and modernize the church's finances. If he doesn't, the Vatican could possibly have no access to the global banking system. That situation would undermine its moral authority and its financial stability.

But it won't be easy, because the Vatican hierarchy is divided into various factions. Some want the church's finances to be more transparent to the faithful and the banking world; others want to keep the church's tradition of secrecy.

So how is the Vatican Bank's finances different from the Catholic Church's?
The church in this context is called the Holy See, which includes the offices of the Roman Curia (the church bureaucracy that makes the wheels turn) and its communications outlets.

In 2011, the Holy See brought in $308 million in revenue, with $326 million in expenditures, for a deficit of about $18 million, according to Catholic News Service.

The budget of the Holy See includes the Vatican Secretariat of State and its diplomatic missions around the world, Vatican councils, the Holy See's investment portfolio and properties, plus the Vatican's newspaper, radio, publishing house and television production.

Most of the Holy See's expenditures were related to personnel costs for about 2,800 employees.

Its revenues included about $61 million from the Vatican bank, which donates its investment profits, contributions from dioceses and religious orders, and financial investment returns.

The United States, Germany and Italy give the biggest contributions every year, according to the Vatican.

How are the Vatican Bank's finances and the Catholic Church's finances different from Vatican City's finances?
Vatican City has its own economy supported by contributions from Roman Catholics around the world, and the sale of postage stamps, tourist fees and mementos.

In 2011, Vatican City's revenues were $113 million, with a surplus of about $27 million, according to Catholic News Service.

Since 2002, its currency has been the euro.

Some gladiators were volunteers who risked their lives and their legal and social standing by appearing in the arena. Most were despised as slaves, schooled under harsh conditions, socially marginalized, and segregated even in death.

They were celebrated in high and low art, and their value as entertainers was commemorated in precious and commonplace objects throughout the Roman world.

The origin of gladiatorial combat is open to debate. There is evidence of it in funeral rites during the Punic Wars of the 3rd century BC, and thereafter it rapidly became an essential feature of politics and social life in the Roman world. Its popularity led to its use in ever more lavish and costly games.

These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.

Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

text:
I'll take your last principle seriously, because it is the right one and because it is the reason I'm reading your seven points instead of dismissing them. 

Which book is judging which. If the Enochic material becomes the lens through which we read Scripture, it fails, and largely it does fail. Your Genesis 3:1 and 2 Corinthians 11:14 framing of that is sound.

But four of the premises under points one through seven do not hold up, and the biggest one is carrying the load for the whole post.

Start with the claim that Jude did not quote a book. The witnesses run the other way, and they are old enough to close the question.

Schodde's 1882 Book of Enoch, the standard English translation from the Ethiopic, states in his General Introduction that Jude's citation "is taken from En. 1:9, and is not a literal reproduction," and his note on 1:9 reads, "This is the verse that is quoted in a free manner in the Epistle of Jude 14 and 15." 

The reason for the "free manner" is visible on the page. Enoch 1:9 has him come "with myriads of the holy to pass judgment upon them, and will destroy the impious, and will call to account all flesh for everything the sinners and the impious have done." Jude 15 has the Lord come with ten thousands of his saints to execute judgment on the ungodly and to convict them of all their ungodly works, "and of all the hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him." That last phrase is Enoch 5:4, where the wicked "have slandered his greatness with high and hard words from your unclean mouths."

Now the Peshitta, which is a second New Testament witness in Syriac. Etheridge's 1846-49 edition reads at Jude 14: "But Hanuk also, who was the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the LORD cometh, with myriads of his saints." "Hanuk" is Syriac for Enoch. "Myriads of his saints" is the Ethiopic wording of Enoch 1:9, not the Greek "ten thousands." And the Clementine Vulgate reads "septimus ab Adam Enoch... Ecce venit Dominus in sanctis millibus suis... et de omnibus duris, quae locuti sunt contra Deum peccatores impii." Three witnesses, and the Syriac and Latin both preserve the Enochic wording rather than a paraphrase.

Your "the seventh from Adam" objection, that Jude identifies a prophet rather than a book, is where I want to give you something you did not have. That phrase is inside the Enochic corpus. Schodde's note on 68:1 reads, "Seventh from Adam, cf. Jude 14," and his own cross-references are to Enoch 65:2, 5, 9 and 67:4. Jude is using a formula the Enochic book supplies. And on your point that Enoch long predates any book, so Jude need not have been reading a volume: the Enochic tradition was in written Hebrew and Aramaic scroll form long before Jude. 

Schodde's own dating puts the Parables, chapters 37 through 71, at roughly 100 to 64 BC as a Hebrew or Aramaic production written in Palestine, and Charles's Book of Jubilees, a second-century BC sectarian work, used the greater part of Enoch 6-16, 23-36 and 72-90, and transmits the Enochic tablets and Watchers tradition itself. 

So the strongest claim is not that Jude might have had a book in hand. It is that the written Enochic tradition was already centuries old and already in circulation when Jude wrote, which is why Jude can quote it in the form the book supplies.

That also disposes of the claim that the appearance was manufactured. A citation of material attested in the second century BC does not require anyone to have edited the text in the first century AD. And the Dead Sea Scrolls are not Gnostic manuscripts. The Qumran library's own sectarian literature affirms a Creator God, the Torah, the temple, sacrificial worship, angels and bodily resurrection. 

Gnosticism denies the Creator and the material creation, so "the scrolls are Gnostic" and "the scrolls are Gnostic origin" are both backwards from what the library actually contains.

Now the points... 

Point one is correct, and I hold it. A prophet's true prophecy does not authenticate a book. Here is what you skipped: the church worked that distinction for centuries. Schodde's General Introduction records that the Fathers, with possibly the single dissenting voice of Tertullian, deny the canonicity of Enoch and properly regard it as apocryphal, "some going even so far as to deny the canonicity of Jude because he had dared to quote an apocryphal work." So "Jude cites Enoch" and "Enoch is Scripture" were never treated as the same claim. Your two claims are real and they were never in tension. 

However, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church still receives 1 Enoch in its 81-book canon, while that same tradition has never treated a canonical book's authority as transferable to everything in the archivist's hands.

Point two falls on the text. 1 Timothy 2:5 concerns the uniqueness of the mediator of salvation and says nothing about whether angels pray for people. Scripture itself shows an angel handling prayers, Revelation 8:3, an angel with a censer offering incense which are the prayers of the saints, and Jude 6 says the holy angels are sent to minister to believers. And in Enoch 40 the intercession belongs to Gabriel, the third voice, and it is explicitly offered in the name of Lord of the spirits. Panuel is the fourth voice, over penitence and the hope of those who inherit everlasting life. You welded the third voice onto the fourth.

Point three misreads the address. Enoch 5 is speaking to unrepentant slanderers. Verse 6 has them giving away their peace for an everlasting curse, and verse 7 continues, "But for the chosen there will be light and joy and peace, and they will inherit the earth, but for you, the impious, there will be a curse." Verse 9 promises the repentant that they will not be punished all the days of their lives and that their lives will become old in peace. Paul calling himself chief of sinners is a man who has been rescued from that category.

Point four is the one I most want to correct, because you reached for it and it does not hold. In 39:1 the "chosen and holy children" descending from the high heavens are the angels, and Schodde's note on the verse says their seed becomes one "not in the sinful manner of the fallen angels and the women, but rather as in 62:14." The text itself separates this union from the watchers' union, which is exactly why Jude 6 and Enoch 6 can stand together without contradiction. 

You also separated "the Book of Enoch" from "the Book of the Watchers" to make your case. The Watchers material is precisely what Jude 6 quotes. Schodde's own note on 12:4 says, "Cf. Jude 6 and En. 15:3 sqq.," and his note on 10:13 routes the same tradition, "cf. Jude 6; 2 Pet. ii. 4," which is the St. Peter link you did not raise.

Point five has the text backwards. Enoch 51:2 says, "And he will choose the just and holy from among them, for the day has come that they be saved." The ones brought out are the righteous, not sinners getting a second chance. And the sequence runs earth and Sheol giving back what they received, the just chosen and saved, the Chosen One arising, the earth transformed, the just living on it. That is closer to Revelation 20:13 through 21 than the contrast you built.

Point six needs a premise the canon never supplies. It has to assume the Enochic Son of man is Christ, and Scripture never makes that identification. On Enoch's own terms, chapters 46 through 48, the Son of man is a distinct figure from the Head of days, a heavenly executor of judgment with a pre-existent name. So the tension you point at is a real difference in how two corpora use a title. It does not amount to Enoch demoting Christ.

Point seven is your best point, and I'll give it to you rather than bury it. The Noah story is striking and it does cheapen the canonical Noah. But it comes from the Noachic fragment, chapters 106 through 108, which Schodde lists among the parts "most certainly foreign to the original groundwork," with 108 "clearly an independent addition." It is a legendary narrative about Lamech's fear, not a claim about Noah's nature, and it has no bearing on the stratum Jude cites.

So your final test is the right test, and the Enochic material Jude cites does not correct the canonical prophets on any point you raised. The real tensions sit inside the corpus, between the early strata and the later Noachic expansion. That is exactly what the Fathers saw when they called the book apocryphal and used it anyway.

Which book is judging which is the right frame. Applied honestly it cuts both ways, and it does not require anyone to choose between "Enoch is worthless" and "Enoch is Scripture."

The first recorded honey trap led to a haircut. Samson was undefeated in battle but swooned before Delilah, who snipped away his locks and stripped him of the secret to his power while he slept.

Jensen Huang’s power lies not in hair, nor even in his trademark leather jacket, but in the sand he taught to think. As founder and CEO of Nvidia, his bet on artificial intelligence built a $4tn empire, yet that fortune offered no defence against an ancient weakness.

On Sunday, Huang confessed to his staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. What might have been dismissed as a private indiscretion instantly turned geopolitical because this generation’s Delilah—Alice Huang—works at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm suspected of siphoning restricted Nvidia chips into China.

The New York Times reported that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her to gather pillow talk on advanced processors and nudge Huang to lobby against trade bans. Beijing naturally dismissed the claim as slander.

Why a hostile intelligence agency would target the billionaire founder of the world’s most strategically vital manufacturer needs little explanation. Virtually every breakthrough shaping the future runs on an Nvidia chip.

These processors carry out the complex calculations that allow computers to mimic human thought, powering everything from consumer chatbots to satellite reconnaissance and missile-targeting systems. Whoever commands these wafers will pull down the old temple and write the next era of human history.

The first prize of such an espionage campaign is the hardware itself. Investigators found that a Malaysian affiliate of Megaspeed purchased $4.8bn worth of Nvidia systems that sat boxed up and uninstalled—classic hallmarks of diversion.

Beyond physical silicon, access to Huang offers direct leverage into the highest corridors of power. Huang frequently visits the White House, talks with the US president, and has already campaigned aggressively to loosen restrictions on selling chips to China.

Customer and invoice data provide another intelligence goldmine. Knowing whether chips are heading to Patriot missile batteries or Western AI labs reveals the private capabilities and strategic intentions of competitors and adversaries alike.

Then there is Taiwan. Huang hails from the island whose foundries at TSMC bring Nvidia's blueprints into physical reality, making him an irresistible focal point for Beijing's strategists.

Even if an operation fails, the downside for Beijing remains negligible. Sowing chaos or triggering the sudden ouster of the world’s most critical semiconductor executive disrupts the supply chain and buys China's domestic foundries crucial time to catch up.

This affair is a blueprint of how China operates, where military, industry, and civil society are treated as one integrated weapon for the Communist Party to deploy.

Under Article 7 of China’s 2017 National Intelligence Law, every citizen is legally obligated to assist state intelligence. Even if the romance began purely out of passion, state security treated it as an operational opening.

Jensen Huang discovered that despite his immense power, his greatest vulnerability was himself. The Ministry of State Security found a weakness and exploited it—and as long as human nature remains unchanged, they will use it again.

A circulating meme claims France, Mexico, and Belgium banned mail-in voting because of fraud—and that several other countries prohibit it altogether.

How much of this is true?

Quite a bit depends on one very important distinction:

Are we talking about ordinary citizens voting by mail within their own country, for any reason, or special arrangements for citizens living abroad?

Those are not the same thing.

Our investigation found that none of the eight individually named countries offers unrestricted, no-excuse domestic mail-in voting to ordinary voters at home.

But some of the meme's historical claims are incorrect or misleading.

✅ FRANCE — THE FRAUD-RELATED BAN WAS REAL

France abolished postal voting in 1975 following documented electoral fraud, particularly in Corsica.

Limited postal voting was subsequently permitted for certain French citizens living abroad. However, France has not restored general no-excuse domestic postal voting.

❌ MEXICO — NO SUBSTANTIATED 1992 FRAUD BAN

Mexico did not abolish an established postal-voting system in 1992 as the meme claims.

It introduced postal voting for eligible Mexican citizens living abroad in 2005, with the first federal overseas postal voting occurring in 2006.

❌ BELGIUM — NO SUBSTANTIATED 2018 FRAUD BAN

Belgium permits postal voting for eligible citizens living abroad.

There is no substantiated evidence of the claimed 2018 fraud-related ban.

📬 SWEDEN, ITALY AND JAPAN

These countries permit postal voting in specific circumstances.

Sweden and Italy allow citizens abroad to vote by mail. Japan permits postal voting for certain voters with qualifying disabilities and eligible citizens abroad.

None offers general, no-excuse domestic postal voting to ordinary voters.

📬 UKRAINE AND RUSSIA

Ukraine does not offer general domestic postal voting.

Russia authorized postal voting through legislation in 2020. However, its use depends on decisions by election authorities rather than an unrestricted right for individual voters to request a postal ballot.

🌎 LATIN AMERICA AND THE MIDDLE EAST

General domestic postal voting is uncommon across these regions.

Argentina illustrates the importance of distinguishing overseas voting from domestic voting.

It introduced overseas postal voting in 2019, repealed it in 2021, and restored it in 2025.

Spain is another important distinction: if the meme's reference to "Latin countries" includes Spain, its domestic postal-voting arrangements contradict the blanket claim.

🇺🇸 HOW DOES THE UNITED STATES COMPARE?

The United States has also allowed eligible citizens living abroad to vote absentee for decades, with federal protections dating back to 1955 and expanded under the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (UOCAVA) of 1986. Like many other countries, the U.S. has long distinguished overseas absentee voting from the broader practice of no-excuse domestic mail-in voting.

As of 2026, 37 states and Washington, DC, permit no-excuse mail-in voting.

Of those:

• 29 states allow registered voters to request mail ballots without providing a special reason.

• 8 states plus Washington, DC automatically mail ballots to active registered voters, although election coverage varies.

• 13 states continue to require a qualifying excuse for ordinary absentee voting.

When did this begin?

No-excuse absentee voting predates COVID-19 by decades.

• 1970: Idaho authorized no-excuse absentee voting.

• 1978: California authorized no-excuse absentee voting.

• 2000: Oregon became the first state to conduct statewide elections entirely by mail.

• 2009: Illinois adopted no-excuse absentee voting.

• 2012–2020: Washington, Colorado, Utah and Hawaii implemented statewide mail-ballot systems.

• 2022: California and Nevada began permanent statewide automatic ballot mailing.

The expansion was already underway before COVID-19, although the pandemic accelerated changes in mail-voting access.

States maintain voter-registration and ballot-verification procedures, but requirements vary.

Some use signature matching, identification numbers, witness signatures, or notarization.

Another important distinction is that the number of detected fraudulent ballots is not necessarily the number of fraudulent ballots that occurred.

Detection depends partly on what officials examine, how thoroughly irregularities are investigated, and whether misconduct can be identified.

That does not establish widespread undetected fraud. It does mean that documented fraud rates and the effectiveness of election safeguards are separate questions worth examining.

⚖️ BOTTOM LINE

None of the eight countries individually named in the meme offers unrestricted, no-excuse mail-in voting to ordinary domestic voters.

France's 1975 fraud-related abolition was real. But the meme also includes unsupported historical claims and overlooks important legal exceptions.

The United States takes a different approach: most states now allow registered voters to request a mail ballot without providing a special reason, or automatically mail ballots to them.

The meaningful questions are not simply whether mail-in voting exists, but who qualifies, what verification is required, and how effectively those safeguards prevent and detect fraud.

text:
Iceberg, Dead Ahead
Back in January, JD Vance stood in a Toledo shipping terminal to defend the Trump economy and grabbed the one metaphor any speechwriter should have struck with a red pen: "You don't turn the Titanic around overnight." Critics quickly pointed out that the Titanic never turned around at all. But give the man his due. He may have given the most honest description of this administration anyone inside it has ever offered.
Ten months later, the ship has found its iceberg. Voters handed Republicans their worst midterm drubbing since Watergate and took both chambers of Congress away from them. Even Vance admits the Iran war cost his party its majority. A captain with any sense would throw the engines into reverse. This one has called for more steam.
Exhibit A: Pete Hegseth. When George W. Bush lost Congress over Iraq in 2006, Donald Rumsfeld was gone the next morning. Asked about his own defense secretary, Trump said he's "doing a very good job." By what measure? Eight months into a war the White House promised would last three or four weeks, there's no achievable objective, no strategy and no off-ramp. Iran choked off the Strait of Hormuz almost as soon as the first bombs fell, and Americans have been paying for it at the pump ever since. On the war's first full day, six Army reservists died at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait. They were in an operations center with a tin roof and no overhead protection, after officers had warned the site couldn't be defended against drones. Hegseth told the Senate that CENTCOM had taken "every possible measure." Their families might beg to differ.
Meanwhile, we're firing $4 million Patriot missiles and $12–15 million THAAD interceptors at Shahed drones that cost Iran $20,000 to $50,000 apiece. The bill topped $47 billion by mid-October, and the stockpiles we'll need for the next fight are running low. None of this should surprise anyone who read his résumé. Under Hegseth, Vets for Freedom raised $8.7 million in a year and spent more than $9 million. Concerned Veterans for America ran deficits and piled up credit card debt on his watch. A man who couldn't balance the books of a small veterans' nonprofit was handed the biggest budget on Earth, and he has spent down our arsenal just as you'd expect.
Exhibit B: immigration. Voters were clear. They didn't want masked agents killing American citizens like Renee Good and Alex Pretti in the streets of Minneapolis. They didn't want neighbors with no criminal record, people who'd lived here for decades, hauled off and disappeared, some of them in the middle of seeking asylum the lawful way. Trump seems to have heard them. On 60 Minutes he allowed that his deportation policy "might be too tough." But two days before that confession aired, he had named Stephen Miller, the architect of that very policy, as his White House chief of staff. Even Republican Sen. Thom Tillis called it "a colossal mistake."
The old wisdom says that when you're in a hole, stop digging. This administration has traded the shovel for the ship's wheel and is steering straight for the ice. You can't teach an old dog new tricks. But you'd think even an old dog would know to get off the boat.

text:
POST OF THE NIGHT, Tuesday 11/10: Minnesota found its quarterback in 24 hours.

If you only read this:
Less than 24 hours after Carson Wentz went 8 of 25 for 81 yards and three turnovers in a 23-6 loss to Buffalo, the Vikings traded a 2027 third-round pick to the Raiders for Kirk Cousins, 38, on NFL trade deadline day.
Las Vegas is moving on to No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza, who starts Sunday against Seattle. The Bills used the day to add safety Amani Hooker, the Chiefs got Josh Downs, and the Colts kept Jonathan Taylor and Daniel Jones.
In the NBA, the Celtics won big in Philadelphia behind Paul George's 36, Giannis Antetokounmpo had 30 and 11 in Miami's win in Utah, and the Knicks beat the Bucks by 32.
In the NHL, Kirill Kaprizov won it for Minnesota in overtime in Montreal on a night the Canadiens honored Carey Price.

Look at the photo. That's Kirk Cousins in a Raiders No. 8 jersey, ball cocked by his ear, in the warmup look he wore for Las Vegas right up until Tuesday afternoon.

1) THE DEADLINE'S LOUDEST DEAL

The Vikings reacquired Cousins from the Raiders on Tuesday, sending a 2027 third-round pick to Las Vegas, per ESPN. Raiders general manager John Spytek said trade talks did not materialize until Tuesday. He said he got a few calls about Cousins before the one that mattered, from Vikings GM Nolan Teasley.

Spytek was open about the choice: "We [were] all staring the future in the face here with Fernando... We had to decide: Do we want to go forward here over the last eight games, or do we want to take what Minnesota is offering right now?"

The timing is the story. ESPN wrote that the deal came less than 24 hours after Wentz turned in the worst performance by a Vikings quarterback since 2006, with a 2.3 QBR. Wentz was filling in for Kyler Murray, who sat out Monday night with a Grade 2 hamstring strain. Murray, who signed a one-year deal with the Vikings this spring, ranks No. 27 in QBR at 45.7.

Cousins played for Minnesota from 2018 to 2023. He threw for 4,547 yards and 29 touchdowns in a Pro Bowl 2022 season, then tore an Achilles in 2023 while playing the Packers. He now has 20 touchdown passes this season, second most in the NFL, with the Raiders. He and Justin Jefferson connected for 5,348 yards in 2020-23, the second most by any QB-pass catcher duo over that span.

The Vikings have lost two straight after a 6-0 start and scored only 19 points in those games. Since the start of 2025, ESPN says, they have the NFL's second-worst team QBR at 36.3. They have used eight different starting quarterbacks since Cousins left in 2024. To make room on the 53-man roster, they released Odell Beckham Jr., who is expected to re-sign to the practice squad, per NFL Network.

2) THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TRADE

Mendoza was officially named the Raiders' starting quarterback. His first career start comes Sunday at home against the Seahawks. He has appeared once, late in a Week 5 loss to New England, going 6 of 8 for 48 yards. Spytek said he "passed every test," and that the move does not mean the 4-5 Raiders are punting on the season.

3) THE REST OF DEADLINE DAY

Bills: Buffalo sent a second-round pick to Tennessee for safety Amani Hooker and a fifth-rounder. Hooker, 28, leads the NFL with five interceptions this season. GM Brandon Beane said talks started about a week ago, stalled, and picked up after he ran into Titans GM Mike Borgonzi at the Notre Dame-Miami game. The Bills beat the Vikings on Monday night and then went shopping.

Chiefs: Kansas City got receiver Josh Downs from Indianapolis for fourth- and fifth-round picks in 2027, with a 2027 seventh coming back. ESPN noted that since Week 4, Patrick Mahomes has not completed a pass of more than 20 air yards. Downs had asked to be traded.

49ers: San Francisco sent a 2027 sixth-round pick to Indy for 34-year-old receiver Keenan Allen. He is seven catches shy of Cris Carter for seventh all-time.

Colts: They traded Downs and Allen, but Taylor and Jones stayed. ESPN reports Indianapolis wanted a first-round pick or equivalent for Taylor, and the Giants had offered a second and a fifth before withdrawing.

Also: Denver got linebacker Daiyan Henley from the winless Chargers for a 2027 fourth and a 2028 fifth. And the Bengals backed out of a deal for Eagles edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie after a hidden cost surfaced: a lost 2027 compensatory third-round pick, per OverTheCap via ESPN.

4) THE NBA

Celtics 123, 76ers 101. Paul George scored 36 on 14-of-22 shooting with six threes. Jayson Tatum had 21. LeBron James had 11 points on 4-of-12 shooting with eight rebounds and five assists. Boston is 9-2, Philadelphia 9-3.

Heat 115, Jazz 109. Giannis had 30 points and 11 rebounds on 12-of-21 shooting. Utah's Darryn Peterson scored 25 and Ace Bailey had 23, but the Jazz fell to 1-10.

Knicks 117, Bucks 85. Jalen Brunson scored 23, Karl-Anthony Towns had 21 points and 16 rebounds, and OG Anunoby made five threes. New York outscored Milwaukee 32-13 in the second quarter and has won four straight. The Bucks lost their seventh in a row and are 1-10.

Suns 133, Clippers 110. Phoenix hit 22 of 43 from 3-point range with seven players in double figures, and the Clippers have lost eight of nine.

Still live when I wrote this: Magic at Kings (Orlando up 88-78 in the fourth) and Thunder at Trail Blazers (tied 49-49 in the second quarter).

5) THE NHL

Avalanche 6, Maple Leafs 3. Gabriel Landeskog scored twice, including the go-ahead goal 5:02 into the third, 51 seconds after Toronto tied it. Toronto has lost four in a row.

Wild 2, Canadiens 1 (OT). Kaprizov scored on the power play 21 seconds into overtime for his 17th goal. Suzuki had tied it for Montreal at 18:22 of the third with the goalie pulled. Price got a nearly four-minute ovation as the Canadiens put him in their ring of honor.

Jets 4, Devils 2. Kyle Connor and Dawson Mercer scored twice each on the night Connor Hellebuyck returned to Winnipeg for the first time since his trade. He did not play, and the crowd booed him anyway.

Capitals 3, Senators 2 (OT). Cole Hutson scored 74 seconds into overtime, set up by Alex Ovechkin.

Also final: Panthers 4, Blue Jackets 1; Blues 3, Red Wings 2.

Still live when I wrote this: Predators led the Kings 2-0 after two periods.

NUMBERS OF THE NIGHT

24: hours between Wentz's 81-yard night and Minnesota's trade for Cousins.
5: Amani Hooker's interceptions, tops in the NFL.
36: Paul George's points in Philadelphia.
21 seconds: how long Kaprizov needed in overtime.

THE THESIS

On Monday night the Vikings had a defense and nobody to hand the offense to. On Tuesday they had a quarterback with a contract, a history in the system and a rapport with their best receiver. Whether Cousins, 38 and coming off two years of recovery from the Achilles, is the answer is a different question. But the Vikings did not wait for the answer to come to them, and the Raiders showed they would rather give the job to the No. 1 pick than keep a placeholder.

The deadline is closed now. The teams that moved, Buffalo, Kansas City, San Francisco and Minnesota, just declared what they think of the next two months.

Is Cousins a real fix for Minnesota's season, or just a better stopgap than Wentz?

The Unseen Government of Organic Form and the Physiological Translation of Reality -

What occurs within a living creature during the infinitesimal interval separating an external impression from its recognition as an intelligible event? An object strikes the retina with reflected light; a distant disturbance becomes a sensation of sound; a dissolved chemical body excites the apparatus of taste; the slightest alteration in temperature becomes a perceptible condition of existence.

Yet none of these external agencies possesses, in itself, the conscious quality eventually apprehended. The body receives one order of phenomena and produces an experience belonging to another. Between them intervenes an immense architecture of surfaces, fluids, membranes, fibres, nervous transmissions, cerebral alterations, associations, and powers whose ultimate relations remained, to Roget, among the profoundest difficulties of natural philosophy.[1]

This remarkable problem supplies the governing principle of the present retrospective investigation. Peter Mark Roget's Treatises on Physiology and Phrenology (1838) preserves an intricate nineteenth-century attempt to describe the operations by which created organic structures receive influences, distinguish impressions, communicate disturbances, maintain their internal equilibrium, generate new tissues, and coordinate processes that no isolated organ could accomplish. Its intellectual apparatus reaches from the minute transformations of albumen and fibrin to the electrical discharges of fishes; from the embryonic appearance of provisional organs to the physiological separation of sensation, remembrance, imagination, volition, and automatic movement. It exhibits the living body as an extraordinarily differentiated system of agencies whose apparent unity conceals an astonishing multiplicity of operations.[2]

The greatest conceptual resource of these volumes lies in Roget's division of the vital powers. Organic affinities govern the characteristic chemical transformations of living substances. Contractility supplies muscular motion. Nervous power transmits influence between distant anatomical regions. Sensorial power designates those physiological changes associated with sensation, thought, and volition. Each exhibits distinctive conditions of operation; their combined action produces a creature capable of occupying space, responding to an environment, preserving its tissues, and experiencing existence.

The classification offers an especially productive historical foundation for investigations into biological information transfer, electromechanical responsiveness, distributed physiological regulation, and the transition between physical excitation and conscious experience.[3]
Here a further possibility emerges, one particularly relevant to the history of artificial intelligence and the technological interpretation of environments. Roget's discussion of sensory reception, nerve conduction, association, and recognition describes an organized sequence in which a surrounding world becomes internally represented through differentiated signals. The external phenomenon is successively received, transformed, transmitted, registered, and associated with previous impressions. The resemblance to later information-processing architectures is conceptual rather than technological, yet the correspondence is striking. An organism possesses multiple channels for the acquisition of environmental differences, while memory and association permit those differences to participate in subsequent activity. In this respect, Roget's physiology affords an early systematic language for problems now associated with sensing, signal integration, adaptive response, and embodied cognition.

The extraordinary electrical apparatus of certain fishes introduces a second order of inquiry. Roget describes regularly arranged membranous prisms, transverse plates, intervening gelatinous material, nervous ramifications, and discharges sufficiently powerful to affect other animals.

Electrical activity appears here as an instrument of the organism, incorporated into a specialized anatomical structure and governed through nervous influence. The body's architecture is capable of accumulating and releasing a physical agency otherwise studied through artificial apparatus. Such descriptions invite a reconsideration of the early history of bioelectricity, the physiological origins of electric instrumentation, and the relation between organic geometry and the directed production of physical effects.[4]

The generative chapters carry the inquiry into another domain of remarkable significance: the appearance of organized form. The primitive trace, blastoderma, vascular area, chorion, allantois, Wolffian bodies, and successive development of the embryo furnish a series of anatomical conditions through which an initially minute living structure acquires differentiated tissues and coordinated functions. Roget's examination of epigenesis, pre-existing germs, syngenesis, and the competing theories of generation preserves an important historical dispute concerning the origin and progression of bodily organization.

A retrospective morphogenetic science can recover from these controversies a sophisticated set of questions concerning the emergence of spatial order, the temporary existence of developmental organs, the relation between vascularization and structural formation, and the regulation of successive transformations.[5]

The comparative physiology of the second volume enlarges this inquiry into extraordinary anatomical territories. Electrical fishes, molluscan nervous arrangements, insect spiracles, amphibian lymphatic hearts, transparent or gelatinous aquatic organisms, and the simple digestive cavities of zoophytes reveal dramatically different ways of accomplishing the functions associated with living existence. Here the investigation encounters what might be called the archipelago of physiological possibilities: innumerable combinations of structure and function, each representing an alternative arrangement of the apparatus through which life operates. Some organisms possess concentrated nervous centres; others distribute their nervous apparatus differently. Some rely on conspicuous organs; others accomplish essential processes through extremely delicate membranes or diffuse tissues. The comparative record therefore offers a catalogue of living architectures far more various than the human body alone could disclose.[6]
A particularly significant philosophical correspondence arises when these observations are placed alongside Ralph Cudworth's doctrine of plastic nature, Francis Glisson's conception of organic irritability, Jan Baptista van Helmont's Archeus, the physiological writings of Georg Ernst Stahl, the formative theories of Caspar Friedrich Wolff and Johann Friedrich Blumenbach, and the nineteenth-century investigations of Martyn Paine. Together these writings preserve different attempts to account for organized action where the immediate causal mechanism was incompletely understood. Roget frequently disputes their explanations, but the disputes themselves become essential evidence for reconstructing the older vocabulary of corporeal agency, formative powers, invisible operations, sympathetic communication, and the relation of soul to animated matter.

The comparative horizon extends further through Emanuel Swedenborg's doctrine of correspondences, Robert Boyle's pneumatical and experimental philosophy, and Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's treatment of hidden natural properties. 

Their conceptual frameworks differ substantially, and those differences are precisely what make them useful. Physiological analogy, spiritual correspondence, experimental causation, and metaphysical agency may be examined as distinct modes of investigating the relations between observable effects and their concealed conditions. Their convergence within a carefully constructed historical research programme opens inquiries into the physiology of ancient natural philosophy, the physical language of spiritual anthropology, and the long history of theories concerning the invisible government of the body.

The resulting investigation is capable of proceeding beyond ordinary descriptive anatomy. It may ask whether particular nineteenth-century observations can be reformulated as experimentally tractable questions about tissue geometry, adaptive biological response, environmental sensing, bioelectric regulation, and the material conditions of conscious experience.

 It may simultaneously examine the historical testimony concerning animal spirits, the Archeus, nervous sympathy, vital principles, mesmeric states, and supernatural interpretations of bodily phenomena, retaining each doctrine within its proper textual and intellectual setting. What appears across these extraordinary volumes is an unusually fertile archive of unfinished questions: an extensive record of problems whose experimental treatment, comparative interpretation, and philosophical consequences remain worthy of sustained investigation.

The scientific importance of this recovery rests upon those individual problems. Some lead toward established fields of physiology and engineering; others support original historical theories; still others furnish hypotheses requiring entirely new investigations. 

Their common value lies in the precision with which the original phenomena can be retrieved, differentiated, and reconsidered.

text:
🌹St. Martin of Tours, Ora pro nobis🌹 

Feast Day - Nov. 11
Saint Martin of Tours was born in Savaria, Pannonia in either the year 316 or 336 AD. That region is what is today the nation of Hungary. His father was a tribune, which is a high-ranking officer in the Imperial Horse Guard. Martin and his family went with his father when he was assigned to a post at Ticinum, in Northern Italy. It is here that Martin would grow up.

Just before Martin was born, Christianity was legalized in the Roman Empire and the bloody persecution of Christians soon came to an end. It was not the official religion of the State, but it could be practiced and proclaimed openly. The Gospel message soon flourished in ancient Rome, transforming the empire. Martin's parents were pagans, but at the age of 10, Martin chose to respond to the call of the Gospel and become a Christian.

At the age of fifteen, Martin was required to follow his father into the cavalry corps of the Roman military. By the time he was 18, Martin is believed to have served in Gaul, and also eventually Milan and Treves. Scholars think he served as part of the emperor's guard.

As a young soldier, Martin encountered a beggar in Amiens. The beggar was unclothed and it was very cold. Martin removed his cloak and with his sword, he cut it in half. He gave this half to the beggar and dressed himself in the remnant. That night, Martin had a vision in which Christ appeared to him. The vision spoke to him, "Martin, a mere catechumen has clothed me." A catechumen is one who is being instructed in the Christian faith. In the early centuries of Christianity, that was a long process of instruction - and Martin was deeply dedicated to it.
About the age of 20, Martin made clear to his superiors that he would no longer fight, following his formed Christian conscience. He refused his pay prior to a battle and announced he would not join in the combat. He became the first recognized conscientious objector in recorded history. His proclamation occurred before a battle near the modern German city of Worms. His superiors accused him of cowardice and ordered that he be imprisoned. Martin offered to demonstrate his sincerity by going into battle unarmed. This was seen as an acceptable alternative to jailing him, but before the battle could occur, the opposing army agreed to a truce and no conflict took place. Martin was subsequently released from military service.

Now out of the military service, Martin could fully dedicate himself to service of Jesus Christ and the Church. He traveled to Tours where he began studying under Hilary of Poitiers, who is now recognized as a doctor of the Church. Martin's studies lasted until Hilary was forced into temporary exile, likely because of his refusal to participate in a political dispute.

Martin then traveled to Italy. According to one account, Martin was confronted by a highwayman and led him to faith in Jesus Christ. Another account tells of Martin confronting the Devil. While on this journey, Martin had a vision which compelled him to return to his mother in Pannonia. He did so and led his own mother to faith in Jesus Christ. Martin attempted to persuade his father to embrace faith in Jesus Christ, but as far as we know, his father refused.

After bringing his mother to the Church, Martin then turned to confronting a growing heresy which was afflicting the faithful and sowing confusion. He became involved in countering the Arian heresy, which denied the divinity of Jesus Christ. The reaction against him was so violent from the Arian leaders that he was compelled to flee. Martin took up residence on an island in the Adriatic where he lived as a hermit for a time.

Martin's teacher Hilary returned to Tours from temporary exile in 361 so Martin traveled there to work and study. Hilary gave Martin a small grant of land where he and his disciples lived.

Martin established a monastery which would be inhabited by the Benedictines.

text:
What you're describing sounds like Medicare Advantage with a Part B giveback. Humana offered me something similar, including a $5,000 dental benefit. Those benefits can be real. They don't prove private insurers are more efficient.

Medicare's independent congressional advisory commission, MedPAC, estimates Medicare pays Advantage plans 14% MORE than traditional Medicare would spend covering those same people.

I've also experienced what your sales pitch leaves out. In Georgia, doctors listed as in-network told me they didn't accept my Advantage plan. Some wouldn't accept ANY Advantage plan. Then there was my MRI: approved, denied, approved again after phone calls, then denied again when the imaging center checked. That's the "efficiency" I experienced.

You also leave out Original Medicare paired with a Medigap policy. That costs an additional premium, but comprehensive policies can cover nearly all remaining costs for Medicare-covered hospital and doctor services, with far fewer prior authorization hurdles.

A premium giveback doesn't mean every service is free or every doctor will accept your coverage. Enjoy your plan, but calling people idiots for pointing out its limitations doesn't make those limitations disappear.

For the record, neither your plan nor the one Humana offered me is necessarily available to someone in the next county over. Where you live determines which plans and benefits you can get.
