text:
The reason your credit card charges you 22% is that back in 1980, Citibank wrote its own law and South Dakota passed it in a single day.

Citi was losing a fortune on credit cards back then. New York capped card interest at 12%, but inflation had pushed what Citi paid to borrow money up near 20%. Their chairman, Walter Wriston, later put it plainly. They were lending at 12 and paying 20, and you didn't have to be Einstein to see they were headed out of business. The card unit had already lost more than $1 billion.

New York wouldn't budge, so Citi's people called South Dakota's governor, Bill Janklow. Four times in one day.

South Dakota was broke. Farmers were paying almost 50 cents a bushel just to haul wheat that sold for $2.20, and the state was already working on getting rid of its interest rate cap. Citi offered 400 jobs if South Dakota would invite its card business in. According to Janklow, Citibank drafted the bill itself, and his legislature passed it in one day.

What made a South Dakota law matter to somebody in Ohio was a Supreme Court case from December 1978. A bank in Nebraska had been mailing credit cards to people in Minnesota at 18%, even though Minnesota capped rates at 12%. The Court sided with the bank unanimously. Whatever state your bank calls home gets to set your rate, no matter where you live.

Delaware passed its own version a year later, and the big New York banks packed up their card operations and moved there. Pretty much every credit card in America has been running on that one-day law for 46 years, which is why state rate caps have mostly been for show ever since.

A federal cap would be the first time the banks had nowhere to move.

Congress has come close before. In November 1991, President Bush mentioned at a fundraiser that he'd like to see card rates come down. The next day Senator Al D'Amato tacked a 14% cap onto a banking bill, and it passed the Senate 74 to 19 after about half an hour of debate. The Dow fell 120 points that Friday, the White House backed away, and the House let it die within days.

Back then the average card charged about 19% while Treasury bills paid 4.6%, so cards ran roughly 14 points above what the government paid to borrow. That was enough to get 74 senators to vote yes in an afternoon. Today the average card that charges interest sits at 22.36%, and the Fed's benchmark rate is under 4%. The spread is bigger now than it was the week the Senate lost its patience.

The politics are weirder this time too. Trump called for a 10% cap back in January. Josh Hawley and Bernie Sanders already have a 10% bill. And Elizabeth Warren is expected to run the Senate Banking Committee when Democrats take over Congress in January.

If something like this actually passes, keep an eye on the fees. In 1980, when Carter froze new credit card signups for a few months, the banks used the moment to start charging a $20 annual fee, and almost nobody canceled. The last time Washington squeezed card pricing, a brand new fee showed up within months.

text:
I gather all crypto sectors favor corporation investment.

Bitcoin, RWA tokenization, stablecoins/payments, and trading/financial infra are the crypto sectors most favored by corporations and institutions.

Capital has concentrated in areas that link to TradFi, offer clear regulatory paths or licenses, generate cash flows, or serve as treasury/operational tools.

[1] Bitcoin = corporate treasuries and store-of-value

Bitcoin is the clearest and most universal corporate conviction asset.

Public companies hold ~1.2-1.3M BTC ~6% of supply, led by @Strategy with ~848,500 BTC.

Other notable holders include @Metaplanet, @MARA, Strive, Galaxy Digital, Coinbase, Tesla, and various miners.

Corporates treat it as a long-term treasury allocation and fiat debasement hedge, often alongside or instead of cash/gold.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs have made institutional access straightforward and sticky.

[2] RWA Tokenization

This is the standout growth narrative for institutions.

Distributed onchain RWA value - excluding pure stablecoins - sits in the ~$35-40B range in late 2026, with strong year-to-date gains.

Tokenized U.S. Treasuries/money-market products lead with ~$15B+, followed by private credit, gold/commodities, and growing tokenized equities.

Major traditional players such as BlackRock’s BUIDL, Franklin Templeton, Circle/USYC, @Ondo, @Securitize, etc. dominate.

Coinbase Ventures lists RWA perpetuals as a top 2026 priority for synthetic exposure to off-chain assets.

Institutions value faster settlement, composability as collateral, and the bridge between TradFi and blockchain.

[3] Stablecoins and Payments

Stablecoins are a core operational and treasury tool.

Corporates and banks use them for cash management, cross-border payments, and faster settlement (including T+0 ambitions).

Regulatory progress (e.g., the GENIUS Act framework) accelerated adoption.

VC funding into stablecoin/payment infra has been robust, and the sector’s share of investment has held steady while more speculative areas cooled.

Banks are piloting tokenized deposits and related rails.

**[4] Trading Infra, CeFi, Exchanges, and Custody**

Galaxy Research data shows Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending consistently attracting the largest share of crypto VC dollars in recent quarters.

This includes institutional platforms, prime brokerage, specialized AMMs, prediction-market terminals, and licensed custody/trading businesses.

Later-stage, revenue-generating, and regulated companies dominate.

M&A has also targeted licenses, payments capabilities, and institutional trading desks.

[5] Institutional / Next-Gen DeFi and Yield

Institutions show interest in staking, lending, tokenized-asset yield, and composable perpetual markets.

Preference goes to compliant, permissioned, or bank-linked versions rather than pure permissionless DeFi.

Pure DeFi VC has cooled, but yield-bearing and TradFi-connected products remain relevant.

[6] AI + Crypto Infra

Select capital flows into AI-related infra, robotics data collection, AI development tools for on-chain work, and related identity/proof-of-humanity solutions.

Coinbase Ventures includes several AI/robotics themes in its 2026 priorities.

This overlaps with broader tech VC trends but is secondary to the finance-linked sectors above.

What Corporations Prefer then?

– Regulatory clarity, licenses, and compliance.

– Revenue or cash-flow positive models over pure speculation.

– Direct links to traditional finance (payments, settlement, Treasuries, custody).

– Liquid, established assets or infrastructure rather than early-stage narrative plays.

Speculative areas like memecoins, pure gaming/metaverse, many pure consumer apps have seen reduced institutional and VC interest relative to prior cycles.

Ethereum and select L1s appear more as thesis-dependent platform bets than universal corporate holdings.

Overall, the pattern is clear to me, best recommend is to focus on these sectors.

text:
Every few decades, someone announces that science has reached its end. In 1903, the revered physicist Albert Michelson wrote that the “facts of physical science have all been discovered.” In the 1980s, Stephen Hawking predicted that theoretical physics might be finished by the end of the century. With the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence, the feeling is in the air again—this time accompanied by a Nobel Prize.

In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind were awarded part of the Nobel in chemistry for their neural network AlphaFold, which predicts the three-dimensional structures of proteins by learning from thousands of experimentally measured shapes. This devilish problem had resisted systematic attacks for half a century; AlphaFold seemed to have solved it once and for all, and the world became fixated on the promise of its approach. Hassabis and his team called AlphaFold “the template for how AI can accelerate all of science to digital speed.” A wave of startups building foundation models for biology, chemistry, and materials discovery raised billions of dollars, buoyed by DeepMind’s success. AlphaFold had shown that the combination of AI and sufficient data could make groundbreaking discoveries (even if we did not understand the underlying mechanisms involved), and it seemed, once again, that a path through the rest of science was laid out before us. 

To be sure, AI will bring extraordinary changes to science, but it has become increasingly clear that AlphaFold, and things like it, may not be the best template for that metamorphosis. Though it is a profound achievement, the conditions that produced the likes of AlphaFold are rare, and the time it will take to meet those conditions in other fields will be measured in decades, not years. Instead, the acceleration of science will come about thanks to another approach: AI agents. 

The primary condition for AlphaFold’s success was the existence of the Protein Data Bank, a data set of roughly 170,000 experimentally validated protein structures on which DeepMind’s team could train its model. The creation of the Protein Data Bank was not simple: It took 53 years of international scientific cooperation and, by a recent estimate, roughly $21 billion worth of experimental work to assemble. Efforts of that scale are infamously difficult to fund, next to impossible to coordinate, and hugely time-consuming to execute; they have often been unsuccessful as a result. 

But even in fields with the requisite cohesion and resources, and where the relevant data are not rendered inaccessible by commercial ownership, another barrier is too little discussed: the scientific impossibility of generating comparable data. In the case of protein structures, the key experimental technique—protein crystallography—is an unusually replicable and dependable tool, so much so that over 25 Nobel Prizes have relied on it. But in most of experimental science, results vary more often than not. Cell lines drift. Chemicals have trace contaminants. Lab humidity changes. The creation of measured datasets that will be consistent enough, accurate enough, precise enough, and scalable enough to train a modern neural network in biology or most of chemistry would require new kinds of measurement and new standardized approaches—none of which will be ready anytime soon. 

Of course, there are a handful of fields where these requirements are met: weather forecasting, much of genomics, very limited areas of chemistry. These may see AlphaFold-style breakthroughs soon, if they haven’t already. Government support for the production and coordination of those datasets will be critical, as the US National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology has argued. But for most open questions in science, we will need a different plan, at least in the short term. Luckily, something quieter and more modest has begun to show promise.

Scientists have always reasoned under uncertainty. Biologists working to identify new drug targets have never had perfect datasets. Instead, they combine docking calculations and known structures, factor in molecular dynamics, run a handful of binding assays, and use their judgment to weigh each method according to its particular strengths and points of failure. The skill of science is not in any single tool; it is synthesizing what many tools produce, and revising the results as the evidence comes in. This is how most working research actually proceeds. But until very recently, no software could do it.

Agents now can. Simply put, an agent is an AI reasoning engine that has been given access to tools—digital or physical—and the capabilities to use them. Over the last few years, a fundamental architectural shift in AI has enabled the rapid proliferation of these programs, which are powered by large language models, dramatically reducing the need for scientifically specialized datasets. For science, this technological advancement represents a foundational change: it has allowed us to create digital tools that can mimic the iterative, highly contingent process of actual research. While tools like AlphaFold apply a powerful approach to a limited question, agents are inherently generalists. They do not represent a new way to do science—instead, they digitally model the human process of discovery. 

Consider Google’s AI Co-Scientist, announced in May. Researchers gave it a one-page brief and a goal: Figure out how antibiotic resistance spreads between bacterial species, a key driver of drug-resistant infections. The system spun up sub-agents. One drafted hypotheses from the literature. Another picked them apart like a peer reviewer. A third ran tournaments to rank the strongest candidates. A fourth refined the winning hypothesis. The agent concluded that resistance genes were hitching rides on bacterial viruses, borrowing whichever virus could ferry them into a new host. The hypothesis was correct. Researchers at Imperial College London had spent a decade reaching the same conclusion through painstaking wet-lab work; their paper, previously unseen by Co-Scientist, was still in peer review.

Agents like Co-Scientist are still novel tools, and there are real challenges to overcome before they become a ubiquitous part of the scientific process: They are still liable to hallucinate, their judgment is not consistent, and they have memory and input constraints that limit the time they can run autonomously. But these technical barriers will fall away, and as they do we will begin to notice the compounding effects of scientific agents on the reliability, consistency, and velocity with which science is done.

Perhaps most notably, agents offer a structural fix for science’s “reproducibility crisis,” the widespread problem of researchers’ inability to replicate each other’s results. For decades, the scientific community has begged researchers to share their raw data and exact code in an effort to standardize experimental processes. But researchers have long resisted this tedious administrative work, which happens after the interesting science is already done. Agents, in contrast, automatically log every move they make, creating an exact record of the method that led to their results and allowing for precise replication. 

A second consequence will be an amplification of scientific memory. The transfer of knowledge between researchers is a famously murky process; if it isn’t done over years of training and observation, graduate students are left to pore through the messy lab notebooks kept by decades of predecessors, looking for the details that will make or break their protocol. As agents become an increasingly large part of the scientific process, though, a lab’s entire scientific history will be recorded in a central, standardized repository of institutional knowledge.

But the most important impact of agents will be speed. In any field, when testing an idea takes less time than arguing about it in a meeting, people stop debating and just run the test. An agent that can read a thousand papers in an hour, design 500 molecules, and learn from its failed tests by morning will bring down the cost of experimentation and fundamentally change the pace at which science gets done. It will also give researchers the freedom to chase bold, strange questions they never would have risked their time on before, opening scientific doors we have yet to imagine.

While the AlphaFold template will certainly be key to incredible discoveries, it alone will not bring us to the end of science. Instead, the shift toward agentic AI represents a much rarer tier of breakthrough: a tool that envelops every field of science at once. Historically, tools of such scope have arrived just a handful of times: calculus, statistical inference, spectroscopy, the computer. Each revealed a world of problems no one had thought to formulate, and those problems, in turn, defined their fields anew. With agents, another such transformation is upon us.

Eric Schmidt was the CEO of Google from 2001 to 2011. In 2024, with his wife Wendy, he co-founded Schmidt Sciences, a philanthropic venture to fund unconventional areas of exploration in science & tech. 

Suhas Mahesh leads AI for Science work at the AI Center of Schmidt Sciences. He is a specialist in AI for materials discovery.

Additional research by Maya Levin, associate and sciences lead, Office of Eric Schmidt.

Cash Generation & Returns: 
Operating Cash Flow (EBITDA-AL minus Capex) jumped 11.6% YoY. Management remains heavily focused on returns, having announced R$ 1.56 billion in shareholder remuneration (Interest on Capital & buybacks) in the first nine months alone.

B2B & AI Innovation: B2B service revenues soared 19.3% YoY over the last 12 months. TIM is also leading in tech efficiency, deploying AI agents in customer service (reducing handling time by 86%) and utilizing AI for predictive network maintenance to prevent outages.

2027E Forecast & Valuation

TIM currently boasts a rock-solid balance sheet, with Net Debt to EBITDA at just 0.78x and Total Net Debt at R$ 11.1 billion.   

At a Q3 closing price of R$ 18.33 (TIMS3) and ~2.378 billion shares outstanding, the Market Cap sits near R$ 43.6 billion. Adding the net debt yields an Enterprise Value (EV) of roughly R$ 54.7 billion. 

Trading at a highly compelling ~3.6x 2027E EV/EBITDA, TIM S.A. offers immense value for a telecom generating double-digit cash flow growth, expanding margins, and paying hefty dividends. It is a pure-play cash machine in the Brazilian telecom oligopoly!

People are saying no new innovations are happening in crypto…

I get your views, I thought the same when I entered the scene after an 18-month-long Zen break..

I started reading ERCs that opened a new chapter for me, which simply screamed how to design better fungible and non-fungible tokens.

Then I thought, what’s up on the privacy side..

I explored some projects like @tacitfi, which managed to pull off the tech with bare minimum initial capital put in by the founder. The tech is novel, making both BTC and ETH private using a ZK rollup..

The tech is validated by some top smart guys, like one of the Ethereum co-founders, @MihaiAlisie.

They are building a proving network too..

ZK proving networks can grow as big as blockchain networks.. I see that future scope.

So the point I want to make here is that it’s all about where we are spending our attention.

The moment you begin to research innovation in crypto, you’re gonna eventually get the whole platter of projects that are doing innovations on bare minimum budgets.

And since we vibecode now, human resource budgets are 90% down, so a project that raises even 10 ETH could make a solid product that could capture revenue in the future.

And if tokens are helping devs raise money, the raised funds should also be allocated to devs with set milestones. That will bring more trust on the dev side.

But we also need to create rules for KOLs and investors where they should be motivated to hold tokens for longer because holding tokens for a longer period should offer either a useful experience or price appreciation..

In some cases, if people love the product, the token becomes the secondary instrument. In those cases, it makes sense not to sell tokens but to hold them for a longer period.

But reaching such a collective mindset on a larger scale looks impossible.

Hence, tokens are not necessary for most projects unless they are using tokens to bootstrap a network that will play an important role in securing, verifying, and achieving trust in products.

text:
Why "bringing manufacturing back" is an economic illusion 🧵👇
Everyone loves talking about bringing low-end manufacturing back home. But let’s look at the basic economic reality: Capital follows efficiency, not nostalgia.
Manufacturing left in the first place for a simple reason: labor and compliance costs were too high. Unless you solve the core issue of labor costs, trying to force a comeback through high tariffs is pure wishful thinking.
Here is why relying on tariff protection is a trap:
1️⃣ Tariffs don't build competitiveness—they cause inflation. High tariffs don't lower local production costs; they just make imports more expensive. Local consumers and businesses end up picking up the tab.
2️⃣ Protectionism creates weak companies. Low-tech manufacturing shielded by government intervention loses its edge. Without free-market pressure, these businesses stop innovating and fail to cut costs.
3️⃣ The inevitable hangover. Government protection cannot last forever. Once the safety net is removed, these artificially supported, uncompetitive industries will collapse—leaving workers and the economy in a far worse position.
Bottom line: High tariffs offer a false sense of security. True manufacturing reshoring only works through high-tech automation—which brings back production, but not the low-skilled jobs politicians promise.

text:
The best clip pages are theme pages.

Theme pages were doing this before “clip page” became the name: choosing a niche, finding ideas worth sharing, and building an audience around them.

Clipping is a format. The page is what gives people a reason to follow.
Here’s how I’d build one now:

1/ Pick the audience, not just the source

Don’t build a page around whichever podcast went viral today.

Build for people who share an interest: business, wealth, tech, fitness, whatever your lane is. Then choose sources that serve those people.

2/ Study what gets people talking

Find the podcasts, interviews, creators, and original posts your audience cares about.

Look for complete answers, strong opinions, disagreements, and useful breakdowns.

Views help you spot attention. Shares, reposts, and comments help you understand what people want to discuss.

3/ Choose the moment without changing its meaning

Skip the unnecessary setup, not the context that makes the answer honest.

One clear thought can be enough. A breakdown might become several clips, or one short clip if the points belong together.

4/ Add a perspective

Why does this matter? What do you agree with? What would you challenge?

Give people something to respond to beyond the borrowed footage. You’re building a page with a point of view, not a folder of highlights.

5/ Build beyond clips

On X, use clips, original posts, and threads.

On YouTube, use Shorts and longer videos. On TikTok and Instagram, use short videos, with carousels where the idea needs more explanation.

The same subject can work across platforms. The execution shouldn’t be identical everywhere.

6/ Give people a reason to come back
Keep the niche clear, the voice consistent, and the content useful. Review what earns shares, reposts, and meaningful comments, then improve the next batch.

7/ Build a business around the audience
A relevant product, service, or resource can help the same people your content already serves.

That’s why we built 7 bots for the whole theme-page operation: business context, planning, research, copy, creative direction, offers, and marketing.

They help you do the work. You make the decisions and publish.

We’re sharing how this works across X, YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram. Clips are part of it. So are threads, carousels, and original content.

The best “clip pages” are theme pages with a new name.

Principal subjects: Divine architecture, sacred light, the exhibition of celestial attributes, the supernatural preservation of Scripture, biblical universality, Mosaic revelation, the tabernacle and Temple traditions, and the diffusion of divine knowledge throughout the nations.
This comparatively short work supplies a striking architectural conception of revelation: Scripture understood as a divinely constructed edifice whose chambers, foundations, illumination, and contents disclose the wisdom of their Architect. 

Volume 2  📜📜

Volume 3 📜📜📜

The surviving title page is particularly remarkable for its juxtaposition of Psalm 14, Genesis 6:5, Ephesians 2:8, and Acts 16:31. These passages establish the work's governing inquiry into the depths of human corruption and the supernatural efficacy of salvation. 

II. 🔑 Scholarly abstract: The Pneumatic Palace, the Counterfeit Image, and the Abyss of the Human Will

A phenomenological investigation into celestial architecture, supernatural cognition, diabolical mimesis, sacred therapeutics, and the hidden operations of redemption

The extraordinary intellectual territory opened by these three historical books concerns the manner in which invisible realities enter the perceptible world, alter the operations of human understanding, and impress their consequences upon memory, affection, conscience, language, architecture, and the disposition of the will. 

William Anderson Scott constructs an immense biblical edifice of transmitted light and manifold chambers; Thomas Brooks anatomizes the artifices by which fallen intelligence disguises its operations beneath apparently desirable objects; James Burdwood examines the mysterious passage from affliction to spiritual consolation; and William Green descends into the abyssus mali, investigating the profound alteration of human faculties and the supernatural principles by which they may be restored.

Scott's architectural philosophy admits of a particularly remarkable comparison with the celestial sanctuary of 1 Enoch 14:8–20. Enoch beholds a house founded upon crystal, surrounded by flames, and overshadowed by the courses of stars and lightning. Beyond the first structure appears a greater and more terrible habitation, containing the throne of divine glory. 

The opposition of crystal and fire, transparency and unapproachable brilliance, establishes an ancient sacred phenomenology in which visibility becomes an instrument of revelation while the divine presence exceeds ordinary perception. Scott's nineteenth-century Crystal Palace, transposed from the international exhibitions of London and New York into a theological structure, acquires an entirely new comparative significance when placed beside this older visionary architecture. The association belongs to our comparative analysis, rather than to a demonstrated borrowing by Scott. Its value lies in the remarkable continuity of architectural forms used to contemplate revealed knowledge, sacred illumination, and the habitation of invisible power. 

The most neglected feature of Scott's address is his optical and pneumatic account of inspiration. The same light, he argues, acquires diversified appearances according to the surfaces upon which it falls. The influence of the Spirit likewise passes through distinct human instruments without surrendering the unity of its originating power. The diversity of inspired authors thus becomes an extraordinary instance of spiritual chromatics: one divine illumination, innumerable intellectual surfaces, and a multiplicity of historically recognizable expressions. His musical analogy extends the conception from light to sound. A common current of air produces different tones through pipes of unlike dimensions. Here lies a sophisticated nineteenth-century analogy for the relation between immaterial agency and the formal peculiarities of created instruments, with immediate applications to biblical linguistics, translation, manuscript history, and the transmission of revelation. The essential material occurs on PDF page 27.

Brooks carries the investigation into the opposite theater of spiritual operation. His demonic adversary works through appearances, disproportionate apprehensions, concealed consequences, counterfeit excellences, and the redirection of legitimate faculties toward destructive ends. Temptation assumes the character of a science of misrepresentation. 

An object remains materially recognizable while its moral significance is altered in the apprehension of its beholder. The devil presents advantage without injury, liberty without captivity, beauty without corruption, and apparent righteousness without the substance of obedience. 

In this respect Brooks's demonology offers a striking parallel with the three nets of Belial described in the Damascus Document, where moral seduction is represented through particularly cunning distortions of conduct and religious judgment. The parallel brings Puritan casuistry into conversation with a much older vocabulary of deceptive spiritual government.

Burdwood introduces a third experimental domain: the troubled heart as the inward chamber where spiritual realities are experienced under conditions of grief, bodily infirmity, remembrance, and expectation. His prefatory account is unusually valuable. He explains that he originally wrote consolations for bereaved families while himself separated from home by sickness; years afterward, overtaken by a severe trial, he rediscovered and benefited from his earlier writing. The document therefore becomes a vessel of counsel transmitted from an earlier condition of the self to a later one. The human mind encounters its own preserved testimony as though receiving instruction across a separation of years. 

This experience invites comparison with the preservation of sacred objects, writings, and life-bearing substances through historical catastrophe in the post-70 CE apocalyptic traditions, especially 2 Baruch and 4 Baruch. The analogy is temporal and phenomenological: what appears dormant or inaccessible may retain a capacity to act at its appointed return.

Green's Abyssus Mali furnishes the metaphysical depth required to unite these inquiries. 

His argument proceeds through the understanding, will, spiritual habit, moral intention, and the formal object of faith. The most revealing distinction is his treatment of what an act is materially and what constitutes it formally. The visible action may be identical while its governing intention produces a different moral judgment. This concerns far more than the classification of behaviors. 

It proposes an invisible morphology of voluntary acts: outward identity concealing inward difference. Green's appeal to Hebrew verbal forms in Psalm 14 also sharpens the question of agency, for he understands the corruption of humankind as involving its own voluntary participation, rather than a simple transfer of responsibility to Adam, the devil, or the Creator.

An especially productive correspondence arises with the Syriac Apocalypse of Baruch, composed in the aftermath of the destruction of Jerusalem. 

In 2 Baruch 54, the responsibility of Adam and that of subsequent human beings are considered together, culminating in the formulation that each individual has become an Adam in his own right. Green's account of personal culpability, separated from his seventeenth-century doctrinal setting and examined alongside this Jewish apocalyptic testimony, reveals an unusually fertile problem: how a primeval act becomes a historical inheritance while each subsequent act remains personally attributable. This is the meeting point of supernatural history, the philosophy of causation, and the anatomy of the human will.
The combined importance of these books culminates in a remarkable sequence. Scott describes the great repository of revelation; Brooks studies the falsification of perception and judgment; Burdwood investigates the restoration of inward equilibrium through divine promises; and Green examines the faculties whose corruption or renewal makes the entire drama possible. 

Together they provide the materials for a substantial historical philosophy of spiritual architecture, deceptive representation, invisible causation, the preservation of sacred knowledge, and the reconstitution of human understanding, illuminated by ancient Jewish apocalyptic literature, Christian Scripture, seventeenth-century philosophical theology, and the extraordinary phenomenological vocabulary preserved in these rare editions.

text:
🎬 : To Kill a Mockingbird
In the quiet geometry of human conscience, where the ordinary acts of daily living collide with the extraordinary demand to choose what is right even when the whole of society has already chosen wrong, there rises a film that does not shout its greatness but simply inhabits it until the viewer is left altered: To Kill a Mockingbird. This is not merely a courtroom drama or a coming-of-age tale set in the dusty streets of Depression-era Maycomb, Alabama. It is the rare cinematic work that treats moral courage as an everyday discipline rather than a heroic flourish, that places the weight of integrity upon a father teaching his children how to live, and that insists the measure of a person is found not in victory but in the refusal to abandon principle when defeat is certain. What makes it stand apart from every other film in its field is the radical simplicity of its claim: that a single man, standing alone against the prejudices of his town, can model for the next generation what it means to do the right thing precisely because it is hard, precisely because most people are against you, and precisely because the easy path is the one that preserves comfort while sacrificing the soul.

Consider the moment when Atticus Finch accepts the defense of Tom Robinson, a Black man accused of a crime he did not commit. The town recoils. Neighbors who once nodded in respect now look away. The children feel the chill of isolation. Yet Atticus proceeds, not because he expects to win, but because the alternative would teach his son and daughter that justice is optional when it becomes inconvenient. Here the film teaches without sermonizing. The lesson is lived: always do the right thing even when most people are against you. Standing up for your values and what is right no matter what, even when it is not easy, becomes the quiet architecture of family life. Scout and Jem watch their father lose the case, watch the jury return a verdict that contradicts the evidence, and still see him walk home with his head level. They learn that integrity is not measured by outcome but by the refusal to bend. In that refusal the film reveals its uniqueness. Other courtroom dramas celebrate the brilliant lawyer who triumphs against odds; this one celebrates the decent man who loses with dignity and still teaches his children that the loss does not diminish the necessity of the fight. It is this willingness to show the cost of principle that elevates it beyond genre conventions and into the realm of moral instruction that feels universal.

The same unyielding honesty extends to the film’s treatment of judgment and appearance. The children spend much of their summer inventing stories about the reclusive Boo Radley, casting him as a monster who lurks behind closed doors. Rumors have shaped their fear. Yet when danger comes in the form of a man who truly means them harm, it is Boo who emerges from the shadows to protect them. The one they judged by the cover of isolation and strangeness proves to be the guardian who saves the ones they love. In that reversal the film offers its brief, piercing reminder: never judge a book by its cover, for those who appear troubled on the outside may carry the quiet goodness that preserves what is most precious. This is not the central drama, yet it completes the moral circle. The same capacity for seeing past surface that Atticus demands in the courtroom is required on the neighborhood street. Everyday life lessons accumulate in small, accumulated acts of looking closer rather than looking away.

What makes the film a masterpiece is the discipline of its craft in service of these ideas. Shot in black and white so that color cannot prettify the moral choices, framed through the eyes of children so that adult hypocrisy is revealed without commentary, scored so that silence carries as much weight as speech, it refuses the easy spectacle that lesser films rely upon. Gregory Peck’s Atticus does not deliver lines as performance; he inhabits a man whose authority comes from consistency rather than charisma. When he delivers his summation, arguing that all men are created equal and that the evidence demands acquittal, the speech is not theatrical triumph but exhausted clarity. The jury still convicts. The audience is left with the knowledge that doing right does not guarantee victory, only the preservation of one’s own capacity to face the mirror. That honesty is what separates it from films that flatter the viewer with triumphant endings. It is why it remains a cultural icon: because it does not ask us to admire a hero who wins, but to recognize the harder heroism of a parent who models for his children how to lose without losing oneself.

The film stands out among others because it trusts the viewer with complexity rather than simplifying for effect. Family is not backdrop; it is the laboratory where values are tested. The porch conversations, the walks home from school, the shared silences after difficult days become the places where lessons are absorbed. Atticus does not lecture his children into understanding empathy; he lives it, and they absorb the living. This is the everyday life lesson that other films rarely attempt: that moral education happens not in grand speeches alone but in the accumulated example of how a person behaves when no one is applauding. The result is a work that feels less like entertainment and more like a sustained argument for the possibility of decency in imperfect circumstances. It is a must watch precisely because the circumstances remain imperfect. Prejudice still exists. Courage is still costly. The temptation to judge by appearance still blinds. The film does not resolve these permanently; it equips the viewer to meet them again.

Behind the making of this enduring work lie details that deepen rather than diminish its power. Gregory Peck read the novel in a single sitting and immediately accepted the role, later traveling to Alabama to meet the man who inspired Atticus, Harper Lee’s father. The town of Maycomb was not filmed in the real Monroeville, which had changed too much; instead an entire Southern community was reconstructed on the Universal backlot using period houses rescued from demolition, so convincing that many viewers believed it had been shot on location. Peck’s lengthy summation in the courtroom was captured in a single continuous take. Harper Lee, upon seeing Peck in character, wept because he even possessed the same slight pot belly as her father; after production she gave him her late father’s gold pocket watch, which Peck carried in his pocket the night he won the Academy Award for Best Actor. Young Mary Badham, playing Scout, became one of the youngest nominees in history for Supporting Actress. Robert Duvall, in his credited debut, played Boo Radley without dialogue, having spent weeks indoors to achieve the proper pallor. These facts do not explain the film’s greatness; they simply confirm that the people who made it understood they were handling something that required fidelity rather than embellishment. text:
You are talking out of the mentality of American extreme institutional decay when there is just husband and wife (“Adam and Eve”) living together in a city and adult children and grandchildren live thousands of miles away from them because they never had formed any strong familial bonds.  But this isn’t true everywhere.  Mr aging and frail parents were always surrounded by 5 of their adult children and 15 grandchildren and a bunch of other relatives who lived within 5 miles of each other.  My mother was too frail to take care of her husband in the last years of his life (8 year age gap) and every time she called me I cancelled all my business appointments and everything else to go and help them, and I was one of 50 other people willing to do that.  And I live within 12 minutes of my mother whenever she calls or needs anything I can drop anything I am doing and go and be with her.  Many times I offered her to live with us she said no.  And if she is incapacitated I will go and physically bring her to my house to live with us.  
I have a very good American friend in Colorado who brought his mother in law to live with them the last 5 years of her frail life.  I literally spend 10’s of thousands of dollars for my kids for their private art and swimming and other schools and miss lots of work hours by homeschooling them and buying them everything they need for their development, and they see it.  3 days ago we were at a big party like high end restaurant with 150 other people all of whom have little or teenage children.  We were the only ones who had taken our kids there, and our kids saw it once again.  Our family is our institution we build.  And you realize that all sorts of misfortunes can happen to people at any time.   You could get into a serious car accident tomorrow and become severely handicapped and your husband would be taking care of you for the rest of your life or his life.  Maybe don’t assume anything.  Those things happen all the time.  My 38 year old neighbor’s 32 year old wife has had serious cancer for the last 2 years and she has been on a wheelchair for that long and the husband is taking care of her.  She was super healthy 2 years ago and now is one step away from the grave.  
In our 10 year marriage there was a year when my wife had serious health issues after we had our second child and I had to stay home and take care of her for 8 months and try to work occasionally.  This year it happened again and I took time off from work for 5 months to find the appropriate clinic and right doctors for her and she finally got well as we figured out what the problem was for her severe allergies.  And I did all that while also full time homeschooling our kids myself.  
I haven’t been resentful towards her, for the things that we had to go thru.  You are being almost resentful for the things that you may or may not go thru in the future.  
If you turn out to be not a terrible mother in law then your children and their spouses will never abandon you, if you even get to live that long.  
But you could just die tomorrow in a car accident by a texting and driving teenage driver and all your pain and worries for the future will go away.

Ukraine has an estimated $15 trillion worth of rare earth minerals underground, along with numerous other natural resources. These resources could be enough to provide the population with the basic necessities of modern society, such as electricity and water, things that not everyone currently has access to.
The state is fighting the war and operating separately, concentrating all resources in its own hands, while the civilian population is constantly under pressure from three different directions, with no compensation provided.
For example, if you left for the EU on the first day of the war, you would be treated as a respected citizen and could receive housing assistance. But if you stayed in Ukraine, you now have to pay twice as much for a safe place to live in Western Ukraine. And if you want a reasonable level of comfort, you end up paying prices comparable to Miami.
International support has declined because Ukraine is no longer constantly in the headlines of major global media outlets, even though the war is now ten times more intense than it was in 2022.

This is unfair. Right now, the destruction of Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, a city of approximately seven million people in the centrer of Europe, is underway through the systematic disruption of electricity, water, medicine supplies and bridges. text:
This clip shows a judge handling a bond request from a defendant with a documented, escalating criminal history: a South Carolina robbery warrant, an open organized criminal activity case, deferred third-degree felony theft, prior evading, criminal mischief, theft, and multiple charges since 2022.

 The defense’s argument is that the defendant is a nursing sophomore at Southern University in Baton Rouge who needs release for Monday finals while currently standing in a Houston courtroom.

The judge’s response is pointed but grounded. He opens by treating jail as a deterrent rather than a hardship to be minimized, then frames the decision around the two standard questions for bond: danger to the public and flight risk. 

The prosecutor’s recitation of escalating conduct (catalytic converter thefts, stolen vehicle, threats) supplies the factual basis for those concerns. When the school claim appears, the judge’s skepticism is not theatrical; a defendant with interstate warrants and recent local charges is asserting an immediate need to travel for exams. That claim requires verification, and the video does not show any offered.

Calling the exchange “humiliation” overstates it. Judges routinely test asserted facts against records; that is the job. Educational aspirations do not automatically outweigh public safety and appearance risks when the record already shows repeated noncompliance and open cases. If the defendant is in fact enrolled and the finals are real, the proper route is documentation through counsel, not an expectation that the court will accept the statement at face value.

 The clip ends mid reading of a magistrate note about an undercover operation, so the ultimate ruling is not shown, but the questioning itself is consistent with ordinary bond analysis rather than personal mockery.

text:
Update: Due to an allergic reaction, the baby was delivered after she lost consciousness - but the sister did not regain consciousness - Naomi's sister 

The life of a popular social media creator, who was folding little pink baby clothes in anticipation of welcoming her first child, fell victim to an unexpected tragic fate within three days. This was 'Naomichan', or Asha Naomi Weerawardhana, who had won the love of thousands of viewers in this country as well as Sri Lankans living in Japan.
Her sudden demise, reported on the night of November 10th, once again confirms the uncertainty of life.

She was eagerly awaiting the day her first child would be born into the world, all while living an extremely beautiful family life. In the video released three days before her death, on November 7th, she was seen, while pregnant, going to baby stores with Kechan and eagerly preparing for the new arrival. However, shattering all those hopes, the news of her demise spread across social media, leaving her audience in unbelievable shock.

With her passing, various rumors regarding the exact cause of death began circulating across social media. Responding to these and explaining the difficult situation she was facing, Naomi's younger sister, Ayesha Weerawardhana, who is studying at Soka University in Japan, joined live on her Facebook account and accurately revealed what had happened.

According to Ayesha, Naomi's death was caused by complications during childbirth. She stated that water remained under the 'water bag', causing an allergic reaction and making it impossible to control the bleeding. For this reason, instead of numbing the mother, doctors completely unconscious her to deliver the baby. Afterwards, doctors made a strenuous effort to revive her. During the doctors' efforts, giving chest compressions from around eleven until about seven, Ayesha mentioned that her brother and she pleaded with her, shouting for her to wake up by her ears. Although tests showed her pulse returned twice at one point, she ultimately could not hold on to life.

Currently, their newborn baby is receiving treatment at another hospital. She expressed her gratitude to everyone who came to the hospital, offered financial assistance, and even sent messages offering to provide breast milk for the baby.

For Ayesha, her sister leaving her alone like this is still like an unbelievable dream. Although she was a popular social media star to many, for Ayesha, she was the loving elder sister who left, entrusting all family responsibilities to her. Ayesha's emotional words, saying "It's like someone stole her, my sister didn't die," perfectly convey the depth of this tragedy that occurred at an unforeseen moment. Ayesha, stating that she doesn't know what to do when she sees the baby equipment hopefully brought to the hospital, thanked everyone who loved Naomi and asked viewers to wish her eternal peace.
